newsitem.title: USA: CBOT corn and soy delivery plan may not pass - trade.
newsitem.headline: CBOT corn and soy delivery plan may not pass - trade.

text.p: Opposition is growing to a Chicago Board of Trade Grain Delivery Task Force proposal to change corn and soybean delivery points and some trade sources say it is unlikely the measure will pass Tuesday's vote.
"The commercials are dead-set against it," said a CBOT floor trader who, like others, declined to be named. "It's going to wreak havoc with barge rates."
CBOT members will vote on Tuesday whether to approve the proposal which would put delivery locations along the Illinois River from Pekin, Ill., to Chicago.
The plan also allows delivery at Burns Harbor, Ind., but eliminates Toledo and St. Louis as delivery points.

The task force was established after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in December told the CBOT that delivery terms of its corn and soybean contracts were no longer suitable due to changes in cash grain marketing. The CFTC said it would make its own recommendations if the CBOT failed to come up with a solution.
CBOT traders and cash sources who oppose the plan say it puts undue emphasis on barges and relies on a single delivery location that can be shut down during inclement weather.

Pit sources said a petition was circulated on the trading floor on Friday, signed by roughly a dozen commercial firms outlining their opposition to the proposal. Among their concerns was concentration in barge ownership which could lead to higher barge rates if the proposal passes, traders said.
But the task force said 21 firms operate the bulk of the barges, and rates are readily available on most news services and from a weekly U.S. Agriculture Department survey.
According to a task force memo released on Friday, there were 11,304 jumbo covered barges owned by 52 firms on the inland river system in 1995.
"While five large firms account for approximately 65 percent of this total, 15 firms operate 100 barges or more," the release states.

"The specification of a shipping certificate as the delivery instrument for the (proposal) provides greater flexibility than warehouse receipts," the memo said. "This increased flexibility will allow deliveries to occur prior to grain being moved into a regular delivery facility."
Countrymark Co-op, an Indiana-based merchandiser with deliverable warehouses in Toledo, issued a statement Friday outlining its opposition to the proposal.

"Farmers, feeders, processors and the entire agricultural community would be damaged by this proposed change," Countrymark chief executive David Swanson said in release. "There is absolutely no reason to close Toledo until the Illinois River idea has an opportunity to be tested."
The task force said Toledo was eliminated to simplify the delivery system and make it more balanced.
Including Toledo would "tip the balance of the delivery system in favor of the seller," the task force said.

"Since the seller is given the option of when and where to deliver, delivery will always occur at the cheapest-to-deliver location where grain is least desirable to the buyer," the task force release states.
Ohio-based merchandiser The Andersons Inc issued a statement last month saying the proposals were "alarming" and needed to be revised. Andersons also has deliverable warehouses in Toledo.

"Making delivery solely along the Illinois River is alarming," said Gary Anderson, president and CEO of The Andersons. "The majority of the river facilities can only load barges. That's a problem if the river freezes or floods or if something happens downstream with the river locks."
The task force contends the river is closed due to weather problems less often than the Great Lakes, which are closed every winter, and the Upper Mississippi River.
